title.narrative: UNDP - Institutional strengthening for FfD and SDGs, INFF 2021-26
UNDP - Institutionsutveckling för utvecklingsfinansiering och SDGs, INFF 2021-26

description.narrative:
The objectives of the intervention have been sligthly up-dated as part of the process of revising and updating the Theory of Change and Results monitoring framework, RMF . The main objective of the proposed up-dated programme by UNDP, is to contribute to the operationalization of the Addis Abeba Action Agenda and progress towards the SDGs at the country level.
A general comment to the up-dated programme document is that the strategic direction of the programme and implementation remains. The revision of objectives and outputs should be seen as an equation of adaptation to learnings and results and is hence adaptive management rather than major changes in direction of programming and implementation.
The proposed programme will support the operationalisation of INFFs to strengthen national financing systems in support of SDG aligned national development plans. The programme will invest in country-level processes and harness knowledge and technical capacity from the international community to help governments and their partners strengthen institutions and overcome technical bottlenecks to financing for sustainable development.
The programme has four outputs, which over the agreement period have been aligned with the overall INFF facility Joint programme framework, and hence adjusted from 3 to 4 components as compared to original agreement (already adjusted in approved workplan and budget for 2023):
1) Governments strengthen collaboration across public and private actors in operationalizing INFFs to ensure national institutional functions are in place to design and implemement inclusive financing policies and reforms.
This is focused on providing support to strengthen the institutions delivering INFFs at the national level with emphasis on building inclusive, multistakeholder approaches.
2) Countries implement financing priorities as identified through INFFs. This is focused on providing technical support and capacity development to governments and their partners at the country level as they develop and operationalize INFFs, identify entry-points and barriers for transforming their financial ecosystems, and deploy SDG financing tools to address them.
3) Governments and their partners access, share and exchange knowledge, insights and tools in support of the operationalisation of INFFs. This is focused on bringing cutting edge tools, knowledge, training, and advocacy (on policy and institutional reform, finance instruments, impact management etc) relevant to the country context.
4) Strengthened agenda setting and coherence across international partners in supporting INFFs - focused on engagement in global processes, and promoting alignment and coordination of support on SDG financing tools and technical support.
There is no change in the assessment of its contribution to Sida's vision 2023, Sida's operational plan 2022-2024 and priorities in the Strategy for Capacity Development, partnership and methods that support the 2030 agenda for Sustainable Development (goal area 1.1, 1.2 and goal area 2).
The programme is well aligned with Sida's vision 2023, the objectives set out in Sida's operational plan 2022-2024 and the priorities in the Strategy for Capacity Development, partnership and methods that support the 2030 agenda for Sustainable development. The intervention has its focus on strengthening country capacity for Financing for Development and Institution building, but aims at the same time to contribute to peer to peer learning and institutional learning at both country and global level.
The intervention has its focus on contributing to the following strategy goals:
1.1. Strengthened institutional capacity of actors in partner countries for sustainable development and poverty reduction.
1.2. Better possibilities and strengthened capacity for actors in partner countries to implment, follow up and participate in the global dialgoue on the 2030 Agenda.
The Intervention also contributes to goal area 2 of the same strategy, with focus on:
Strengthened capacity and leadership, greater knowledge and engagement among a range of actors, including Swedish actors, ability to contribute to the global implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

UNDP har inrättat en INFF - facilitet för att stödja länder att stärka de nationella finansieringssystemen till stöd för nationella utvecklingsplaner anpassade efter Agenda 2030. INFF-faciliteten kommer att genomföra insatser under en treårsperiod i en portfölj av länder. Genom faciliteten strävar UNDP efter att investera i processer på landsnivå och utnyttja kunskap och teknisk kapacitet i olika länder och från det internationella samfundet att hjälpa regeringar och deras partner att stärka institutionerna och övervinna tekniska flaskhalsar till finansiering för hållbar utveckling. INFF-faciliteten bör ses som ett sätt att samla expertutlåtanden och stödja länder på ett systematiskt och konsekvent sätt kring finansiering för utveckling. UNDP placerar partnerskap med andra FN-organ, internationella organisationer och utvecklingspartners samt inom finans- och utvecklingssektorerna som avgörande för INFF:s slutnäring.UNDP investerar i dessa partnerskap som en del av sin tjänsteleverans, i syfte att säkerställa att olika aktörer samarbetar för att stödja landsledda strategier för att finansiera hållbar utveckling. Att fördjupa och etablera partnerskap är en integrerad del av själva förändringsteorin och hörntonen i genomförandestrategin.

UNDP has established an INFF facility to support countries to strengthen national financing systems in support of SDG- aligned national development plans. The INFF Facility is set to deliver interventions over a three year period in a portfolio of countries. Through the facility, UNDP aim to invest in country-level processses and harness knowledge and technical capacity across countries and from the international community to help governments and their partners strengthen institutions and overcome technical bottlenecks to financing for sustainable development. The INFF facility should be seen as a way to gather expertice and to support countries in a systematic and coherent way around finacning for development. UNDP places partnerships with other UN agencies, international organizations and development partners as well as across the finance and development sectors as critical to the INFF endevour. UNDP invests in these partnerships as part of its service delivery, with a view to ensuring that different actors work together in support of country led approaches to financing sustainable development. Deepening and establishing partnerships is an integral part of the theory of change itself as well as the cornerston of the implementation strategy.

description.narrative:
The below headings summarizes Sida's reflections on result achievement and the partnership on INFFs throughout 2023. Through support of the INFF Facility, Sida has contributed to:
A shift of focus from INFF preaparation and analysis of financial flows to implementation and reform:
The first phase of the work with INFFs have centered around the architecture for an integrated approach to financing for development. As countries are advancing their INFF work and developing financing strategies, there is an ongoing shift on country level (and in the way the INFF facility needs to support) from analysis, architecture and preparations to reforms and implementation. The revised results framework and the adjusted data points for the INFF survey have enabled further analysis and results linking to financing strategies. This new data is being compiled (during Q12 2024) in a stocktaking report on financing strategies. Some results that can be highlighted from the early and emerging analysis of financing strategies are:
- A growing number of countries have established and are implementing countryled, impact oriented financing strategies encompassing public and private finance a transformation from just five years ago when most national sustainable development plans had no financing strategy. - Governments are using these financing strategies to embed the SDGs into the national financial architecture, charting a course to unlock investment for a new, more sustainable and inclusive growth path. Initial data (from the INFF survey, prepared by UNDP in a draft analysis of financing strategies) based on a selection of emerging reforms in 18 countries show more than $16bn in resources leveraged for SDG investment and enhanced SDG-alignment and scope for alignment of more than $27bn in existing resources.
- A growing number of countries are using their financing strategy as a platform for integrated policymaking on financing for development, climate and nature outcomes other countries can learn from this approach to leverage synergies and efficiencies in financing across climate, nature, gender equality and many other priorities. - There are signs of increasing alignment among international partners behind countryled financing strategies: this should be accelerated, with further commitment to do so set out in the revised Financing for Development agenda. Sida should further explore how alignment can be taken into account in strategy implementation.
Examples of results: Initial signs from the implementation of INFFs are promising. Thirteen national and subnational governments have a working financing strategy and more than fifty countries are implementing reforms shaped through their INFF. These reforms are embedding sustainable development into government budgets, financial markets and private sector operations. They are catalysing pipelines of SDG-aligned investment opportunities and deploying new and innovative SDG-aligned financial instruments. And they are strengthening governance and institutions, deepening transparency, accountability and collaboration for more inclusive and sustainable financing.
The first fruits of these reforms are starting to emerge. Analysis of some of the reforms implemented by seventeen of these countries finds $16 billion in new finance leveraged for investment in sustainable development and alignment and scope for alignment of more than $32 billion.
In public finance, thirtytwo countries are advancing changes to embed sustainable development priorities in the design, implementation and monitoring of public expenditure. In Bangladesh, for example, climate change is now a core part of budget documentation from the initial budget call circular to KPIs for budget programmes and expenditure reports to parliament and the government recently used this system to access a $1.4 billion loan from the IMFs Resilience and Sustainability Facility. In Colombia the government established a tagging system that has seen SDGaligned budget expenditure grow by 17% in four years, an increase of $10 billion.
On the tax front, countries are prioritising changes to both increase revenue mobilisation and align tax policy with sustainable development priorities. Kyrgyzstan, for example, has introduced a new tax code to strengthen the effectiveness and SDGalignment of tax incentives worth an estimated 5% of GDP.
Regarding sovereign debt, many countries are innovating to issue or refinance debt in ways that sustainably unlock capital for investment in sustainable development. Benin, for example, was the first LDC to issue an SDG bond, unlocking €500 million for investment in social sectors, environment projects and other areas. Indonesia has mobilised more than $8 billion through a range of diversified issuances, most recently including an inaugural sovereign blue bond. Building on these changes, INFFs can become a platform for an integrated approach to public finance. Many governments are already using the approach to look at climate change within their tax policy, debt systems and expenditure structures at the same time. Extending this to consider the integrations, synergies and tradeoffs across them, and applying a similar approach through the lens of gender equality, nature and other crosscutting priorities will be an important next step.
In private finance, countries are placing a strong emphasis on hardwiring sustainability into the foundations of financial markets. Taxonomies are being established in many contexts to provide a common framework for understanding the contributions of private finance to climate, green, social and sustainable development priorities. Standards and capacity for disclosure and reporting frameworks are enhancing transparency and accountability for the impacts firms have on sustainability. In Thailand, for example, the SEC recently introduced guidance for SDG impactbased reporting within the sustainability reporting requirements for listed firms with a combined market capitalisation of over $480 billion. Over time and as capacity is built the intention is for this to evolve from a voluntary to mandatory reporting requirement. Countries such as Cabo Verde are also innovating in the deployment of new financial instruments. The Stock Exchange of Cabo Verde launched BluX, the worlds first blue economy sustainable finance platform, which has mobilised more than €35m through various issuances to date.
At the same time, countries are promoting investment in specific areas that are catalytic for SDG progress. Many countries have been developing market intelligence on investment opportunity areas with high SDGimpact potential and promoting investment in Nigeria, for example, firms in a $175m pipeline of projects are being equipped to mobilise investment.
Blended finance and PPPs are being used to scale up investment in key areas and expand the impact of private capital by ensuring enhanced access for last mile populations. In Senegal, for example, credit guarantees from the African Development Bank are facilitating €400 million for green and social investment while the Uganda Development Bank has established a Climate Financing Facility providing affordable finance for climatesmart agriculture, infrastructure and lowcarbon industry.
Overall, analysis of just a selection of reforms from only 17 countries highlights approximately $16 billion in new finance leveraged and the enhanced alignment and scope for SDGalignment of more than $32 billion of financing (UNDP calculations). These are just the first among a larger pipeline of policy reforms being shaped at the country level to further align the financial system for sustainable development.
It is Sida's assessment that the emerging results are well in line with the ambitions of the INFF facility in response to the Addis Abeba Action Agenda and well responds to the support provided by Sida. Furher assessment of results will be made as the Annual report is submitted in June 2024 (for FY 2023).
Institutional development is critical: The progress on INFFs over 2022/2023 has shown how critical institutional development is to the sustainability and success of the INFF process. Examples of experiences and results have been provided in the Annual report for 2022 from e.g. Belize and Mongolia. Sida has asked UNDP to further advance the analysis of the work and mandate of the INFFfacility in relation to institutional reform, not the least in relation to formal and informal institutions constraining public private partnerships to materialize. The INFF partner meeting of 2024 therefore had a focus on/ deepdive in the area of institutional development. Sida's Unit for Capacity development (CAPDEV) participated in the meeting and shared experiences of how Sida is approaching institutional development and support through capacity development.
The ongoing dialgoue with the INFF facility on a robust approach to institutional development is important and we have seen it advance throughout 2023. There is however need to continue efforts including consolidating approaches. It will be key to also bring DESA into this dialogue in relation to developing and learning from INFF experiences/ countries. The events and stocktaking taking place during 2024 will be a good stepping stone for this, for example the launch of the INFFstocktaking report at a side event in FfDforum NY april 2024 and the OECD side event and dialogue on scaling up of technical assistance from DAC members can contribute to broadening the discussion to partners outside of the facility and most importantly, to engage in dialogue with developing countries about how the global community can better respond to needs of institutional development to scale financing for development.
Role of financial market participants and collaboration with investors within GISD: In the Annual report from 2022 (submitted and assessed by Sida during 2023) evidence is provided, highlighting the need for strengthened multistakholder approaches and collaboration with financial market participants to scale financing for development. This also clearly links to enabling environment for financial markets and institutional development as mentioned above. As stated in the emerging analysis from the INFF survey from 2023: The financial sector is the intermediary to direct financing from where the capital is available to where it is needed. It should play a critical role channelling financing towards the areas where there are greatest SDG investment opportunities. Yet, efforts have typically focused on the financial impact of policies, for example increasing foreign direct and portfolio investment flows in monetary terms with little regard to SDG impact of the financing flows. Results from emerging implementation of financing strategies show several examples of the importance of scaling development of financial markets and strengthen SDG alignment.
During 2023, Sida has supported the INFF initiative through, among other things, connecting the work (and countries) of INFFs with the investor alliance also supported by Sida, GISD. GISDs working group on SDG bonds have during 2023 developed guidelines and best practice for SDG bonds and Sida has connected INFF countries to the work to ensure a comprehensive country perspective into the guidelines and to secure that best practice/ guidelines developed to scale/ SDGalign investments matching country priorities. Exept for facilitating and brokering the connection and dialogue between GISD and INFF countries within the scope of the working group, Sida has also taken initiatives to policy dialogue at key events, for example in the margins of UNGA 2023 (luncheon at the UN rep with Swedish Minister for Development cooperation and trade hosting and several GISD investors present). The launch of the guidelines in 2024 will also further lead to a consultation process between countries and investors. Through this engagement, Sida has stressed the need for a strong and loud voice of developing countries to allow for clarity on country priorities expressed through INFFs (and linked financing strategies) in relation to scaling investments for SDGS and underscoring development effectiveness principles.
Enhanced focus on Climate, environment and biodiversity During 2023 Sida and UNDP/the INFF facility have jointly engaged to explore and share knowledge around how climate finance can be scaled as part of integrated approaches to financing. Climate finance is moving towards integrated financing as a strategic imperative for achieving the Paris Agreement, while financing strategies already are incorporating climate action. This is evidenced by the emerging results of the INFF survey which states that the number of climate oriented reforms currently comprise approx. 20% of all financing reforms in those countries where financing strategies are already being operationalized. More than 10 countries are currently piloting this joint agenda linking INFFs to NDCs.
In February 2024 Sida, as part of the annual meeting, introduced a deep dive on environment and climate to better understand (and jointly learn) how the INFFs are capturing climate ambitions and experiences from linking NDCs to INFFs. The event provided a first occasion to learn and understand country requests in relation to INFFs. Sida participated through the regional team in Kenya, the Embassy in TZ as well as Sida HQ policy specialist from INTEM. It provided a great opportunity to focus on experiences and the conclusion from the meeting was that a next step is to follow up on country level. Sida and UNDP will hence, during 2024, jointly invite TZ and KE respectively to explore opportunities to engage in country INFFs including understanding opportunities within the climate space (and scaling synergies between Sida's global support to INFFs and bilateral support to TZ and KE).
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
